When an article is published we post the peer reviewers’ comments and the authors’ responses online. 
We also post the versions of the paper that were used during peer review. These are the versions that 
the peer review comments apply to.

For peer review only
3
ABSTRACT
Objective: Antibiotics are one of the most commonly prescribed medications. They disturb 
normal gastrointestinal flora, which can lead to diarrhoea. Probiotics are non-pathogenic live 
micro-organisms thought to improve the microbial balance of the gastrointestinal tract and 
reduce colonisation by pathogenic bacteria. Our objective was to evaluate existing evidence 
for the use of probiotics in preventing antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in adults.
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis.
Data sources: We performed a literature search of the electronic databases CINAHL Plus, 
EMBASE, MEDLINE (Ovid), and Web of Science from database inception to September 
2019 as well as hand searching of trial registries and reference lists of related reviews.
Study selection: Two independent reviewers identified whether randomised controlled trials 
met the following inclusion criteria: adult population, a probiotic (any species, formulation or 
dose) intervention, placebo or no treatment control, incidence of antibiotic-associated 
diarrhoea as the outcome. 
Data extraction and synthesis: Two reviewers independently collected data and assessed 
risk of bias using a pre-constructed data extraction form. For pooled data, if 
I2 was less than 
25% we used a fixed effects model; if I2 was 25% or greater we used a random effects 
model. Sub-group analyses were performed to evaluate species-specific and dose-specific 
response. 
Results: Thirty-seven studies (total 9799 participants) were included in this review. The 
pooled analysis suggests that co-administration of probiotics reduces the risk of antibiotic-
associated diarrhoea in adults by 46% (Odds ratio (OR)=0.54 [95% CI: 0.44, 0.67], 
p<0.00001). In sub-group analyses, high dose compared with low dose of the same probiotic 
formulation demonstrated a positive protective effect (OR 0.53 [95% CI: 0.33, 0.84], p<0.01), 
and certain species particularly of the lactobacillus and bifidobacteria genera were found to 
be effective.
Conclusions: Our data suggests that probiotics are effective for preventing antibiotic-
associated diarrhoea. Secondary analyses of higher dosages and certain species have 
shown increased effectiveness.

STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY
 Comprehensive literature search encapsulating seven years of new data since a 
comparable meta-analysis was last published by Cochrane
 Included only studies reporting on incidence of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (AAD). 
Analysis of the effect of probiotics on duration of AAD may provide information about 
reducing severity.
 Significant heterogeneity between studies; significant variability in species and dose 
of probiotic interventions, start date and duration of co-administration of probiotics, 
baseline health of participants and antibiotics administered

For peer review only
5
INTRODUCTION
Antibiotics are one of the most commonly prescribed medications worldwide. They disturb 
normal gastrointestinal flora [1] and a common consequence is diarrhoea [2]. This leads to 
prolonged hospital admissions [3], increased morbidity and mortality [4] and greater costs to 
the health system [5,6]. Antibiotic associated diarrhoea (AAD) has been reported in 5-35% of 
patients receiving antibiotics, varying with the type of antibiotics, the general health of the 
patient and their exposure to pathogens [7].
Probiotics are non-pathogenic live micro-organisms, thought to improve the microbial 
balance of the host and reduce colonisation by pathogenic bacteria. They can be delivered 
orally, adhere to target gastrointestinal epithelium and are stable in acid and bile (Dunne et 
al. 2001). Probiotics are increasingly available in capsules, powders and fermented milk 
drinks and are promoted in health food shops and supermarkets, and in the media, for a 
multitude of purposes.
It is suggested that probiotics are the panacea to AAD. This would be a very attractive 
solution to an expensive problem with significant morbidity. Several mechanisms are 
proposed to contribute to the protective effect of probiotics against AAD. Antibiotics are 
known to disrupt the complex balance of gastrointestinal flora, allowing colonisation by 
pathogenic organisms such as 
Clostridium difficile (C. difficile). Probiotics are believed to 
temporarily colonise the gut, producing bactericidal acids and peptides, and competing for 
nutrients and epithelial adhesion. Several species of the 
Lactobacillus genus are acid 
producing, lower environmental pH, and secrete exotoxins that inhibit pathogenic bacterial 
growth and inhibit binding of enterotoxins to gut epithelium [8–11]. Probiotics, particularly 
species in the 
Lactobacillus and Saccharomyces genera, are also reported to upregulate 
both the innate and adaptive immune systems through multiple mechanisms [12–15].
It is estimated that the increase in hospital admission due to AAD is 3.6 to 21.3 days [16,17]. 
One of the most expensive probiotics in Australia costs less than four dollars daily (VSL#3 
AU$3.96 per day, available from NourishMeOrganics.com.au, April 2020). This is negligible 
compared to the cost of one day of Australian inpatient care, which according to 2017 data 
cost on average $2128 (Independent Hospital Pricing Authority, 2019). 
Our hypothesis has been extensively investigated. In a Cochrane review [19] authors found 
moderate quality evidence for a large protective effect of probiotics against Clostridium

For peer review only
6
difficile-associated diarrhoea (CDAD) (RR 0.36; 95% CI: 0.26, 0.51). Although C. difficile is 
the most common infectious organism isolated, in most cases of AAD no causative agent is 
found. Faecal analysis indicates incidence of C. difficile to be 20% [20], or less [21]. 
Furthermore while probiotics significantly reduce incidence of CDAD they do not appear to 
reduce 
C. difficile infection [19]. Goldenberg and colleagues suggest that the role of 
probiotics may be more in alleviating the symptoms of infection rather than preventing 
colonisation itself. For this reason, we examined the protective effect of probiotics against 
the occurrence of AAD without any specific causative organism.
The primary objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate existing 
evidence for the protective effect of probiotics against AAD in adults. Secondary objectives 
were to examine dose-specific and species-specific response; comparing different doses of 
the same probiotic and looking at the effectiveness different probiotic species in preventing 
AAD.
METHODS
Eligibility criteria
Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing probiotic use (any strain, dose or 
formulation) to placebo, alternative dose, alternative probiotic strain, or no treatment, for the 
prevention of diarrhoea in adults receiving antibiotic therapy were eligible for inclusion in this 
review. Studies were excluded if they examined probiotics for treatment, rather than 
prevention, of AAD. Studies of adults, receiving any antibiotic therapy for a course of any 
length, or for any reason, were included. Studies of paediatric populations were excluded. 
The primary outcome measure was incidence of AAD, classified as three or more episodes 
of loose stools (5-7 Bristol Stool Scale), in any 24-hour period during the antibiotic treatment 
or follow-up phases. 
Information sources and search strategy
A comprehensive electronic search (Appendix A) was performed of CINAHL Plus, EMBASE, 
MEDLINE (Ovid), and Web of Science from database inception to September 2019. The 
search was broad to include as many individual probiotic genera as possible and all clinical 
indications or outcomes (full search terms in Appendix A). Clinical trial registers including 
ClinicalTrials.gov and the Australia New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ANZCTR) were 
also searched, as well as hand searching of reference lists of relevant systematic reviews

For peer review only
7
and included studies. The search was limited to RCTs in an adult population written in 
English and already in publication.
Study selection
Two of three of the authors (CG, GK and KL) independently assessed each study for 
inclusion in the review. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion.
Data collection process and data items
Data were extracted from each article by two of three of the authors (CG, GK and KL), using 
a standardised data extraction form following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic 
Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines[22]. This was housed within Covidence 
online software (Covidence systematic review software, Veritas Health Innovation, 
Melbourne, Australia. Available at www.covidence.org). Data items collected included the 
number of patients allocated to each group, the probiotic species, formulation, dose and 
regime, whether a placebo or ‘nothing‘ control was used, and outcome data on incidence of 
AAD.
Risk of bias in individual studies and risk of bias across studies
The quality of the evidence was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias [23] tool within 
the Covidence online software. The domains assessed were allocation concealment, 
blinding of participants, personnel and outcome assessors, incomplete outcome data, 
selective outcome reporting and other sources of bias.
Summary measures and synthesis of results
The odds ratio (OR) was calculated for outcome measures for categorical data. A sensitivity 
analysis was performed, and the 
I2 statistic was reported. Where the I2 was less than 25% a 
fixed effects model was used, or if it was 25% or greater a random effects model was used.
Patient and public involvement
There was no patient or public involvement in this study.

Study selection and characteristics
A total of 346 articles were identified in the initial search, of which 53 were eligible for full-
text review, and 37 of those articles were eligible for inclusion in the study. Thirteen of these 
were published after the Cochrane review mentioned previously [24]. The PRISMA flow-
diagram (figure 1) displays the study selection process and the citations and characteristics 
of each included study are presented in table 1.

Placebo
All included studies were RCTs, conducted in adult populations. The age range was from 18 
to 85 years. Interventions were comparable, in terms of all being probiotic formulations, 
however, there was variation in the dose and species of probiotic used as well as the 
probiotic formulation i.e. tablets, powder, yoghurt or fermented milk drink. We investigated 
these by sub-group analysis. All studies reported the outcome of interest; incidence of AAD 
as measured by three or more occurrences of diarrhoea in a 24-hour period, however, this 
was not the primary research question of the trial in all cases.
Risk of bias within studies
The risk of bias was assessed for all outcomes as described in the Cochrane Handbook 
[23]. The risk of bias summary is displayed in table 2. Overall 51% of studies were rated as 
having a low risk of bias, while 49% were at unclear risk of bias. No study was deemed to be 
at high risk of bias overall. Risk of bias due to missing data was considered to be very low 
given that all studies reported outcomes on incidence of AAD.
Table 2: Summary of risk of bias assessment
Overall, 23 trials lacked adequate information to assess the overall risk of bias. Almost half 
of the RCTs reported only the probiotic genus and species that were used but not the strain 
(17/37), and many did not state whether treatment allocation was concealed (21/37) or failed

11
to report an intention-to-treat analysis (21/37). However, 19 of the 37 trials reported that both 
participants and outcome assessors were blind to the intervention. In a further five studies 
either participants or assessors were blinded. There is some risk of bias due to clear lack of 
blinding in 8% of the trials and possibly in a further 41% of the trials which did not clearly 
report on blinding.
Results of individual studies and synthesis of results
Of the 37 studies included (table 1), 31 were placebo-controlled, seven provided ‘no 
treatment’ as the comparison - one study compared their treatment group with both a 
placebo group and a no treatment control [57]. Three trials compared two probiotic arms of 
differing dose with a control group [36,41,47]. Where there were two treatment groups (e.g. 
high dose and low dose) and one control group, the control group was split so that half 
served as comparator for each arm, in accordance with the Cochrane Systematic Review 
Guidelines [61]. Similarly in one study [32] where a probiotic group was compared with a 
placebo and ‘no treatment’ control, the probiotic group was split. Only one study was found 
to compare two strains of the same probiotic species, however, it was excluded as it was not 
randomised [62].
The overall pooled results of the 37 studies (reporting on 9799 participants) (Figure 2), 
comparing probiotics with a placebo or no treatment control, demonstrated a statistically 
significant reduction in the incidence of AAD by 46% (Odds ratio (OR)=0.54 [95% CI: 0.44, 
0.67], p<0.00001). This suggests that the number needed to treat (NNT), to prevent one 
case of AAD would be 19 patients. There was significant heterogeneity (
I2=58%), therefore 
we used a random effects model for analysis. 
Subgroup analyses
When sub-group analyses were performed, where probiotics were compared to placebo, 
and probiotics were compared to no treatment, both demonstrated a significant reduction in 
risk of diarrhoeal incidence of 39% (OR=0.61 [95% CI: 0.49, 0.75], p<0.00001) and 65% 
(OR 0.35 [95% CI: 0.21, 0.60], p<0.001) respectively. There was significant heterogeneity 
(I2=50% and 59% respectively), therefore analyses used a random effects model.
Subgroup analysis: probiotic dose
Three studies directly compared high dose and low dose of the same probiotic [36,41,47]. 
The combined higher dose group demonstrated a significant reduction in the incidence of

control group, so to include this data in the complete case analysis the control group was 
halved to create a comparator for each arm, as described above.
Subgroup analysis: probiotic species
Most studies used probiotic formulations containing more than one probiotic species so a 
sub-group analysis was performed on all individual species mentioned in included studies 
(Table 3). Where only one study existed, using a particular strain, we used that study’s 
outcome data alone. The following probiotic strains demonstrated significant reduction in 
AAD when compared to control: 
L. acidophilus, L. bulgaricus, L. casei, L. helveticus, L. 
paracasei, L. reuteri, L. rhamnosus, Lactobacillus spp., S. boulardii, B. longum, B. 
licheniformis, and B. subtilis. However, L. plantarum, B. animalis ssp. lactis, B. bifidum, S. 
thermophilus and C. butyricum showed no improvement in AAD compared to control.

Adverse effects
No serious adverse events were reported in any of the included studies. Two studies 
reported a significantly greater number of non-serious adverse events in the probiotic group 
compared with the control group in their respective trials [29,57].
Small study effects
On inspection, the funnel plot of the complete case analysis (Figure 3) shows little evidence 
of publication bias. This suggests that our results are robust to theoretical large future trials 
with results in the opposite direction (i.e. that probiotics increase the risk of AAD rather than 
decreasing it).
DISCUSSION
Summary of evidence
The principal finding of this review is that probiotics significantly reduce the risk of AAD 
(OR=0.54 [95% CI: 0.44, 0.67], p<0.00001), with a NNT of 19 patients. These results were 
similarly positive in sub-group analyses, with high doses more effective than lower doses, 
and some species more effective than others. As is the nature of systematic reviews, we 
found significant heterogeneity between study designs and population, severity of illness of 
the study group, as well as probiotic species used, dose, timing and duration of probiotic 
administration.
Our results show evidence of a placebo effect, with a reduction in AAD incidence of 39% 
(OR=0.61 [95% CI: 0.49, 0.75], p<0.00001) when probiotics were compared to placebo, but 
65% (OR 0.35 [95% CI: 0.21, 0.60], p<0.001) when probiotics were compared to no 
treatment. Placebo effect is not well understood but this could be attributed to expectations 
of symptom change with neurobiological underpinnings and actual effects on the brain and 
body [63]. This effect could be investigated further in well-designed, three-armed, RCTs.

14
Secondary objectives included sub-group analyses of dose-response and species-specific 
response. In studies where dosages of the same species were compared [36,41,47], higher 
doses showed a significantly greater benefit (OR 0.53 [95% CI: 0.33, 0.84], p<0.01). It is 
difficult to interpret the dosage effect as the three studies that compared different doses of 
the same probiotic species made comparisons of differing magnitudes. 
Many studies used blends of probiotic species, which made it difficult to establish 
independent associations. In our sub-group analyses, the individual probiotic species that 
demonstrated the greatest effect sizes were 
B. longum (3 studies, OR=0.14 [95% CI: 0.05, 
0.43], p<0.001), L. bulgaricus (4 studies, OR=0.32 [95% CI: 0.19, 0.55], p<0.0001) and L. 
paracasei (3 studies, OR=0.43 [95% CI: 0.22, 0.86], p<0.05). Although not demonstrating 
the same magnitude of effect, L. acidophilus (17 studies, OR=0.62 [95% CI: 0.47, 0.82], 
p<0.001), L. casei (9 studies, OR=0.51 [95% CI: 0.33, 0.79], p<0.01) and S. boulardii (9 
studies, OR=0.56 [95% CI: 0.37, 0.84], p<0.01) were used in many more studies. Overall, 
we have seen that the lactobacillus genus shows a good effect with a small confidence 
interval. The individual species 
L. acidophilus was used in the greatest number of studies, 
showing a significant effect with a relatively small confidence interval. A significant effect 
size was noted in some of the other species which may be worth looking into more 
specifically in future trials. L. plantarum, B. animalis ssp. lactis, B. bifidum, S. thermophilus 
and C. butyricum did not show evidence of effectiveness in reducing incidence of AAD. 
One study [62] compared two strains of L. casei, Actimel® (L. casei DN-114001) and 
Yakult® (L. casei Shirota), for the prevention of AAD. In this study L. casei DN-114001 was 
significantly more effective than L. casei Shirota, however, we were unable to include this 
data in our review as it was not randomised. Future RCTs should focus on direct 
comparisons of single or combined probiotic species.
The most commonly identified indication for antibiotics was treatment of H. pylori. In the five 
RCTs investigating adjunct probiotic use with antibiotics for H.pylori treatment we found a 
reduction in diarrhoeal side-effects (OR=0.43, [95% CI: 0.27, 0.69], p<0.001).
A treatment schedule was reported in most studies (34/37) with duration from five to 56 
days. The largest proportion (13/37) of studies reported probiotic administration for the 
duration of antibiotic therapy plus a further seven days. As duration of antibiotic use also 
differed between studies there was quite a range in duration of probiotic use. It would,

15
however, be biologically plausible to suggest that probiotic use should be continued for a 
period after the cessation of antibiotics. This is another question worth investigating in future 
trials.
Limitations
A limitation of this study is that the only outcome measured was incidence of diarrhoea. This 
review’s utility in clinical practice may have been improved by also analysing duration of 
AAD. Additionally, it may have been informative to correlate outcomes with the duration of 
probiotic course or the date of probiotic initiation in relation to antibiotics.
This study was somewhat limited in scope as we did not include grey literature, 
correspondence with authors about trials currently in progress or to obtain missing data, and 
only included studies published in English.
Agreements and disagreements with other studies
This study is concordant with findings from the aforementioned Cochrane systematic review 
[19]. Goldenberg found that probiotics led to a significant reduction in incidence of AAD from 
21% to 13% of participants (RR 0.60; 95% CI 0.49 to 0.72). The present review included 13 
additional trials (7567 additional participants) published after the Cochrane review. This 
increase in total population increases the power of our review to detect smaller clinically 
relevant differences between groups in incidence of AAD. 
Our sub-group analyses found similarly to one previous meta-analysis [64] that 
Lactobacillus 
and Saccharomyces genera reduced incidence of AAD. A more recent meta-analysis [65] 
found, also concordantly, that most Lactobacillus and Bifidobacteria species and S. boulardii 
were effective. Previous meta-analyses have not reported on dose-response. 
Contrary to the findings of our review, one meta-analysis [66] reported that probiotics may 
not be effective in reducing the incidence of AAD, however, only 13 studies were analysed, 
including adults over 65 only. This suggests a need for looking separately at the 
effectiveness of probiotics in populations of younger and older adults.
CONCLUSIONS
Page 16 of 30
For peer review only - http://bmjopen.bmj.com/site/about/guidelines.xhtml

For peer review only
16
This review provides evidence of a protective effect of probiotics against AAD (OR=0.53 
[95% CI: 0.42, 0.67], p<0.001). In absolute terms, the NNT, to prevent one case of AAD 
would be 19 patients. In studies that compared dosage of the same probiotic higher doses 
were found to be significantly more effective. The probiotic species that demonstrated the 
greatest effect were 
B. longum, L. bulgaricus and L. paracasei but were each only studied in 
a handful of trials. The species L. acidophilus, L. casei and S. boulardii, although 
demonstrating relatively smaller effect sizes, were used in many more trials focusing on 
prevention of AAD. The species that did not demonstrate a significant effect in the 
prevention of AAD were L. plantarum, B. animalis ssp. lactis, B. bifidum, S. thermophilus and 
C. butyricum. 
This review has demonstrated overall effectiveness of probiotics for the prevention of AAD, 
including a dose-response and some species-specific effectiveness of probiotics. However, 
further high-quality trials are needed, focusing on direct comparison of doses, comparison of 
individual species and combinations of species. Future studies should record not only 
incidence of diarrhoea, but also duration and associated length of stay in hospital so that an 
assessment of the cost-benefit of probiotic therapy can be made. Trials should ensure that 
adequate blinding and reporting of adverse events is included.

not access any information that could lead to the identification of an individual patient, no 
concerning ethical issue was raised in this research. Therefore, obtaining ethical approval 
and consent of participants was waived.

For peer review only
PRISMA 2009 Checklist 
Section/topic  # Checklist item  Reported 
on page #  
TITLE   
Title  1 Identify the report as a systematic review, meta-analysis, or both.  1 
ABSTRACT   
Structured summary  2 Provide a structured summary including, as applicable: background; objectives; data sources; study eligibility criteria, 
participants, and interventions; study appraisal and synthesis methods; results; limitations; conclusions and 
implications of key findings; systematic review registration number.  
2 
INTRODUCTION   
Rationale  3 Describe the rationale for the review in the context of what is already known.  3 
Objectives  4 Provide an explicit statement of questions being addressed with reference to participants, interventions, comparisons, 
outcomes, and study design (PICOS).  
3 
METHODS   
Protocol and registration  5 Indicate if a review protocol exists, if and where it can be accessed (e.g., Web address), and, if available, provide 
registration information including registration number.  
NA 
Eligibility criteria  6 Specify study characteristics (e.g., PICOS, length of follow-up) and report characteristics (e.g., years considered, 
language, publication status) used as criteria for eligibility, giving rationale.  
4 
Information sources  7 Describe all information sources (e.g., databases with dates of coverage, contact with study authors to identify 
additional studies) in the search and date last searched.  
4 
Search  8 Present full electronic search strategy for at least one database, including any limits used, such that it could be 
repeated.  
4 / 
Appendix  
Study selection  9 State the process for selecting studies (i.e., screening, eligibility, included in systematic review, and, if applicable, 
included in the meta-analysis).  
4 
Data collection process  10 Describe method of data extraction from reports (e.g., piloted forms, independently, in duplicate) and any processes 
for obtaining and confirming data from investigators.  
4 
Data items  11 List and define all variables for which data were sought (e.g., PICOS, funding sources) and any assumptions and 
simplifications made.  
4 
Risk of bias in individual 
studies  
12 Describe methods used for assessing risk of bias of individual studies (including specification of whether this was 
done at the study or outcome level), and how this information is to be used in any data synthesis.  
4 
Summary measures  13 State the principal summary measures (e.g., risk ratio, difference in means).  4 
Synthesis of results  14 Describe the methods of handling data and combining results of studies, if done, including measures of consistency 
(e.g., I2) for each meta-analysis.  
4

For peer review only
PRISMA 2009 Checklist 
Page 1 of 2  
Section/topic  # Checklist item  Reported 
on page #  
Risk of bias across studies  15 Specify any assessment of risk of bias that may affect the cumulative evidence (e.g., publication bias, selective 
reporting within studies).  
4 
Additional analyses  16 Describe methods of additional analyses (e.g., sensitivity or subgroup analyses, meta-regression), if done, indicating 
which were pre-specified.  
4 
RESULTS   
Study selection  17 Give numbers of studies screened, assessed for eligibility, and included in the review, with reasons for exclusions at 
each stage, ideally with a flow diagram.  
5 
Study characteristics  18 For each study, present characteristics for which data were extracted (e.g., study size, PICOS, follow-up period) and 
provide the citations.  
5 
Risk of bias within studies  19 Present data on risk of bias of each study and, if available, any outcome level assessment (see item 12).  6 
Results of individual studies  20 For all outcomes considered (benefits or harms), present, for each study: (a) simple summary data for each 
intervention group (b) effect estimates and confidence intervals, ideally with a forest plot.  
7 
Synthesis of results  21 Present results of each meta-analysis done, including confidence intervals and measures of consistency.  7 
Risk of bias across studies  22 Present results of any assessment of risk of bias across studies (see Item 15).  8 
Additional analysis  23 Give results of additional analyses, if done (e.g., sensitivity or subgroup analyses, meta-regression [see Item 16]).  8 
DISCUSSION   
Summary of evidence  24 Summarize the main findings including the strength of evidence for each main outcome; consider their relevance to 
key groups (e.g., healthcare providers, users, and policy makers).  
8 
Limitations  25 Discuss limitations at study and outcome level (e.g., risk of bias), and at review-level (e.g., incomplete retrieval of 
identified research, reporting bias).  
9 
Conclusions  26 Provide a general interpretation of the results in the context of other evidence, and implications for future research.  10 
FUNDING   
Funding  27 Describe sources of funding for the systematic review and other support (e.g., supply of data); role of funders for the 
systematic review.  
11 
 
From:  Moher D, Liberati A, Tetzlaff J, Altman DG, The PRISMA Group (2009). Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta -Analyses: The PRISMA Statement. PLoS Med 6(6): e1000097. 
doi:10.1371/journal.pmed1000097  
For more information, visit: www.prisma-statement.org.

APPENDIX A: SEARCH STRATEGY FOR ELECTRONIC DATABASES 
 
 
Databases:  EMBASE, Medline (Ovid), Web of Science 
Plus grey literature, hand searching, search of trial registries Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry 
(ANZCTR) and ClinicalTrials.gov

For peer review only
3
ABSTRACT
Objective: To evaluate existing evidence for the use of probiotics in preventing antibiotic-
associated diarrhoea (AAD) in adults.
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials (RCTs).
Data sources: We performed a literature search of the electronic databases CINAHL Plus, 
EMBASE, MEDLINE (Ovid), and Web of Science from database inception to May 2021 as 
well as hand searching of trial registries and reference lists of related reviews.
Study selection: Two reviewers identified whether RCTs met the following inclusion criteria: 
adult population to whom antibiotics were administered; a probiotic intervention; a placebo, 
alternative dose, alternative probiotic strain or no treatment control; and incidence of AAD as 
the outcome.
Data extraction and synthesis: Two reviewers independently collected data and assessed risk 
of bias using pre-constructed data extraction forms. We used a random effects model for all 
analyses. Sub-group analyses were performed to evaluate species-specific and dose-specific 
response.
Results: Forty-two studies (11,305 participants) were included in this review. The pooled 
analysis suggests that co-administration of probiotics with antibiotics reduces the risk of AAD 
in adults by 37% (Risk ratio (RR) =0.63 [95% CI: 0.54, 0.73], p<0.00001). The overall quality 
of the evidence using the GRADE criteria was found to be moderate. In sub-group analyses, 
high dose compared with low dose of the same probiotic demonstrated a positive protective 
effect (RR 0.54 [95% CI: 0.38, 0.76], p<0.01), and only certain species, mainly of the 
lactobacillus and bifidobacteria genera, were found to be effective. Studies with a low baseline 
AAD risk did not show any difference in risk but studies with moderate or high baseline AAD 
risk demonstrated a significant risk reduction.
Conclusions: Probiotics are effective for preventing AAD. Secondary analyses of higher 
dosages and certain species have shown increased effectiveness. Our results may not be 
applicable in clinical scenarios of lower baseline AAD risk.

5
STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY
 An updated literature search encapsulating four years of new data since a comparable 
meta-analysis was last published by Cochrane in 2017
 We calculated and reported the number needed to be treated with probiotics to protect 
one person from antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (AAD), so that our data can be easily 
interpreted by patients and clinicians
 This meta-analysis looked only at incidence of AAD, but clinical applicability may have 
been improved by collecting data on duration and severity of AAD as well as length of 
stay in hospital and quality of life measures
 There was complexity in combining results due to substantial heterogeneity between 
study methodologies and outcome measures

For peer review only
6
INTRODUCTION
Antibiotics are one of the most prescribed medications worldwide. They disturb normal 
gastrointestinal microbiota [1] and a common consequence is diarrhoea [2]. This leads to 
prolonged hospital admissions [3], increased morbidity and mortality [4] and greater costs to 
the health system [5,6]. Antibiotic associated diarrhoea (AAD) has been reported in 5-35% of 
patients receiving antibiotics, varying with the type of antibiotics, the general health of the 
patient and their exposure to pathogens [7].
Probiotics are live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a 
health benefit on the host [8]. They are believed to improve the microbial balance of the host 
and reduce colonisation by pathogenic bacteria. They can be delivered orally, are thought to 
adhere to target gastrointestinal epithelium and are stable in acid and bile (Dunne et al. 2001). 
Probiotics are increasingly available in capsules, powders and fermented milk drinks and are 
promoted in health food shops and supermarkets, and in the media, for a multitude of 
purposes.
Several mechanisms are proposed to contribute to the protective effect of probiotics against 
AAD. Antibiotics are known to disrupt the complex balance of gastrointestinal microbiota, 
allowing colonisation by pathogenic organisms such as 
Clostridium difficile (C. difficile ). 
Probiotics are believed to temporarily colonise the gut, producing bactericidal acids and 
peptides, and competing for nutrients and epithelial adhesion. Several species of the 
Lactobacillus genus are acid producing, lower environmental pH, and secrete exotoxins that 
inhibit pathogenic bacterial growth and inhibit binding of enterotoxins to gut epithelium [9–12]. 
Probiotics, particularly species in the Lactobacillus and Saccharomyces genera, are also 
reported to upregulate both the innate and adaptive immune systems through multiple 
mechanisms [13–16].
It is suggested that probiotics are the panacea to AAD. This would be a very attractive solution 
to an expensive problem with significant morbidity. It is estimated that the increase in length 
of hospital stay due to AAD is 3.6 to 21.3 days [17,18]. One of the most expensive probiotics 
in Australia costs less than nine dollars daily (VSL#3 probiotic formulation, AUD $8.60 per 
day, April 2021). This is negligible compared to the cost of one day of Australian hospital 
inpatient care, which according to 2017 data, cost on average $2128 [19].

For peer review only - http://bmjopen.bmj.com/site/about/guidelines.xhtml

For peer review only
7
Our hypothesis has been extensively investigated. In a Cochrane review [20] authors found 
moderate quality evidence for a large protective effect of probiotics against Clostridium 
difficile-associated diarrhoea (CDAD) (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.52). Although C. difficile is 
the most common infectious organism isolated, in most cases of AAD no causative agent is 
found. Faecal analysis indicates incidence of 
C. difficile in AAD to be 20% [21], or less [22]. 
Furthermore while probiotics significantly reduce incidence of CDAD they do not appear to 
reduce 
C. difficile infection [20]. Goldenberg and colleagues suggest that the role of probiotics 
may be more in alleviating the symptoms of infection rather than preventing colonisation itself 
[20]. For this reason, we examined the protective effect of probiotics on the occurrence of AAD 
without any specific causative organism.
The primary objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate existing 
evidence for the protective effect of probiotics against AAD in adults. Secondary objectives 
were to examine dose-response and species-specific response in preventing AAD.
METHODS
Eligibility criteria
Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing probiotic use (any strain, dose or formulation) 
to placebo, alternative dose, alternative probiotic strain, or no treatment, for the prevention of 
diarrhoea in adults receiving antibiotic therapy, were eligible for inclusion in this review. 
Studies of adults, receiving any antibiotic therapy for a course of any length, or for any reason, 
were included. Studies of paediatric populations were excluded. The primary outcome 
measure was incidence of AAD, as defined by authors, during the antibiotic treatment or 
follow-up phases. Studies were excluded if they examined probiotics only for treatment, rather 
than prevention, of AAD. We limited included studies to those written in English as our group 
did not speak any other languages.
Information sources and search strategy
A comprehensive electronic title search (Appendix A) was performed of CINAHL Plus, 
EMBASE, MEDLINE (Ovid), Web of Science and Google Scholar from database inception to 
May 2021. The search was broad to include as many individual probiotic species as possible 
and all clinical indications or outcomes (full search terms in Appendix A). Grey literature and 
clinical trial registers including ClinicalTrials.gov and the Australia New Zealand Clinical Trials 
Registry (ANZCTR) were searched, as well as hand searching of reference lists of relevant 
Page 8 of 48
For peer review only - http://bmjopen.bmj.com/site/about/guidelines.xhtml
BMJ Open

For peer review only
8
systematic reviews and included studies. The search was limited to RCTs in an adult 
population.
Study selection
Two of three of the authors (CG, GK and KL) independently assessed each study for inclusion 
in the review. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion.
Data collection process and data items
Data were extracted from each article by two of three of the authors (CG, GK, KL), using a 
standardised data extraction form following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic 
Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines[23]. This was housed within Covidence 
online software (Covidence systematic review software, Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, 
Australia. Available at www.covidence.org). Data items collected included the number of 
patients allocated to each group, the probiotic species, formulation, dose and regime, whether 
a placebo or ‘nothing‘ control was used, and outcome data on incidence of AAD.
Assessment of risk of bias in individual studies and overall quality of the 
evidence
The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias [24] tool within the Covidence 
online software. The domains assessed were sequence generation, allocation concealment, 
blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessors, incomplete outcome 
data, selective outcome reporting and other sources of bias (e.g. differences in baseline 
characteristics or funding of trials by pharmaceutical companies). Assessment was conducted 
by two of three authors (CG, GK, KL) and discrepancies resolved by consensus. The overall 
quality of the evidence was rated using the GRADE approach [25] independently by two 
authors (CG, KL) and consensus reached through discussion.
Statistical analysis and measures of treatment effect
For data analysis we used the RevMan 5.4.1 statistical software (Review Manager (RevMan) 
[Computer program]. Version 5.4. The Cochrane Collaboration, 2020.) Using a random-effects 
model, dichotomous data were reported as a risk ratio (RR) with corresponding 95% 
confidence intervals (95% CI). The number needed to treat (NNT) was also calculated for the 
complete case analysis. The 
I2 statistic was reported for statistical heterogeneity, although

clinical and methodological heterogeneity would not have been reflected within this test.  Our 
a priori clinical heterogeneity variables included: probiotic dose, probiotic species and risk of 
bias. We also conducted post hoc  sub-group analyses on baseline risk for our primary 
outcome, incidence of AAD, and concurrent use of probiotics with H. pylori eradication. 
Sensitivity analyses were performed where deemed necessary.
Patient and public involvement
There was no patient or public involvement in this study.
RESULTS
Study selection and characteristics
A total of 356 articles were identified in the initial search, of which 60 were eligible for full-text 
review, and 42 of those articles (11,603 participants) were eligible for inclusion in the study. 
Five of these were published after the Cochrane review mentioned previously [20]. Figure 1 
summarises the PRISMA flow of studies. The characteristics of each included study are 
presented in table 1.

All included studies were RCTs, conducted in adult populations. The overall age range was 
from 15 to 85 years. Interventions were comparable, in terms of all being probiotics, however, 
there was variation in the dose and species of probiotic used as well as the probiotic 
formulation i.e. tablets, powder, yoghurt or fermented milk drink. We investigated these by 
sub-group analysis. All included studies reported on the outcome of interest; incidence of AAD, 
however, this was measured differently between studies and was not the primary research 
question of the trial in all cases.
Risk of bias within studies
The risk of bias summary is displayed in figure 2. Six of the 42 studies were rated as having 
a low risk of bias, while 36 were rated as having a high or unclear risk of bias. On sensitivity 
analysis, the low risk of bias studies demonstrated no protective effect of probiotics (RR=0.78, 
[95% CI 0.57, 1.07], p=0.13) as opposed to the high or unknown risk of bias studies (RR 0.59, 
[95% CI 0.50 to 0.70], p<0.00001). 
Results of individual studies and synthesis of results
Of the 42 studies included (table 1), 33 were placebo-controlled and eight provided ‘no 
treatment’ as the comparison. One study compared their treatment group with both a placebo 
group and a no treatment control [62]. Four trials compared two probiotic arms of differing 
doses with a control group [38,43,49,66]. Where there were two treatment groups (e.g. high 
Page 13 of 48

13
dose and low dose) and one control group, the control group was split so that half served as 
comparator for each arm, in accordance with the Cochrane Systematic Review Guidelines 
[67]. Similarly in one study [34] where a probiotic group was compared with a placebo and ‘no 
treatment’ control, the probiotic group was split. In one study [62] the placebo milk contained 
a higher concentration of starter strains than the probiotic milk. We combined the groups to 
make it an overall treatment group, which the authors had done themselves in the 'both' group, 
compared with a ‘no treatment’ group. Only one study was found to compare two strains of 
the same probiotic species, however, it was excluded as it was not randomised [68].
The overall pooled results of the complete case analysis of 42 studies (reporting on 11,305 
participants) (Figure 3), comparing probiotics with any control, favoured probiotics 
demonstrating a statistically significant reduction in the incidence of AAD. The pooled risk ratio 
of 0.63 (RR=0.63 [95% CI: 0.54, 0.73], p<0.00001) indicates that those who took probiotics 
were over one third less likely to develop AAD. This data suggests that the NNT, to prevent 
one case of AAD would be 20 patients. Statistically significant heterogeneity was detected for 
this comparison (P<0.00001; 
I2=60%). We used a random effects model for this analysis 
based on the heterogeneity of the study methodologies. 
Sub-group and heterogeneity analysis
When sub-group analyses were performed, where probiotics were compared to placebo 
(RR=0.69 [95% CI: 0.60, 0.80], p=0.0004), and where probiotics were compared to no 
treatment (RR=0.35 [95% CI: 0.27, 0.47], p<0.00001), a significant reduction in relative risk of 
diarrhoea was noted (Forest plots available in supplemental files). The difference in effect size 
may be explained as placebo effect.
Across all of the sub-group analyses, the I2 statistic ranged from zero to 78%. There was also 
substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, therefore we used a random effects 
model for all analyses. There was substantial variation in the AAD definition employed in the 
included studies (Table 1). Although 13 studies defined AAD as ≥3 loose stools (5-7 Bristol 
Stool Scale) in 24 hours, 12 defined AAD as ≥3 loose stools (5-7 Bristol Stool Scale) in two 
days or more, 11 studies used various other definitions of AAD and five studies made no 
mention of their definition.
Sub-group analysis: probiotic dose

Four studies directly compared high dose and low dose of the same probiotic [38,43,49,66]. 
The higher dose group demonstrated a significant reduction in the relative risk of AAD (RR 
0.54 [95% CI: 0.38, 0.76], p=0.0004) (Forest plot available in supplemental files). 
Sub-group analysis: probiotic species
Most studies used probiotic formulations containing more than one probiotic species so a sub-
group analysis was performed on all individual species mentioned in included studies (Table 
2). Where only one study existed that used a particular strain, we analysed that study’s 
outcome data alone. The following probiotic strains demonstrated significant reduction in AAD 
when compared to control: 
L. acidophilus, L. bulgaricus, L. casei, L. paracasei, L. rhamnosus, 
Lactobacillus spp., S. boulardii, B. animalis ssp. Lactis, B. longum, B. licheniformis, B. subtilis 
and Bacillus clausii.  However, L. helveticus, L. plantarum, L. reuteri, B. bifidum, S. 
thermophilus and C. butyricum provided no improvement in AAD compared to control.

Sub-group analysis: Concurrent H. pylori  treatment
In the seven RCTs investigating adjunct probiotic use with antibiotics for H. pylori treatment 
we found a reduction in diarrhoeal side effects of 45% (RR=0.55, [95% CI: 0.41, 0.73], 
p<0.0001) (Forest plot available in supplemental files).
Sensitivity analysis: Baseline risk of AAD
In a post hoc analysis we divided our included studies into low (0-10%; 7 studies), moderate 
(11-30%; 21 studies) and high (>31%; 14 studies) baseline risk of AAD. The pooled studies 
with a low baseline risk of AAD did not show any difference in risk, but trials enrolling 
participants with a moderate or high baseline risk for developing AAD demonstrated 39% 
(RR=0.61, [95% CI: 0.48, 0.78], p<0.0001) and 45% (RR=0.55, [95% CI: 0.46, 0.66], 
p<0.00001) risk reduction respectively (Forest plots available in supplemental files).
Sensitivity analysis: High/unknown risk of bias
To examine for robustness we pooled data from the studies which we assessed as low risk of 
bias in all domains, and separately pooled the studies which scored high or unknown risk of 
bias in any domain. In our sensitivity analysis with the high and unknown risk of bias studies 
removed, the protective effect of probiotics against AAD was no longer statistically significant 
(RR=0.78 [95% CI: 0.57, 1.07], P =0.13). However, with only the high risk of bias studies 
removed from the complete data set, a similar pooled protective effect of probiotics was found 
(RR=0.65 [95% CI: 0.54, 0.78], p<0.00001) (Forest plots available in supplemental files).
Adverse events
Of the 42 included studies, 32 reported on adverse events. No serious adverse events were 
reported in any of the included studies. One study reported four (2.0%) non-serious adverse 
events in the probiotic group compared with none in the control group [30] and another

Small study effects
On inspection, the funnel plot of the complete case analysis (Figure 4) is symmetrical which 
suggests little evidence of publication bias. 
Overall quality of evidence
Using the GRADE approach [25] we rated the overall quality of the evidence as moderate. 
Although all included studies were RCTs, many demonstrated design limitations, mainly 
reflecting the reporting of sequence generation and allocation concealment in older studies, 
which suggests some risk of bias. This was balanced, however, by a good magnitude of effect 
and dose-response gradient, increasing the certainty of this body of evidence.
DISCUSSION
Summary of evidence
The principal finding of this review is that probiotics significantly reduce the risk of AAD in 
adults, with an NNT of 20 patients. These results were robust in sub-group analyses, with high 
doses more effective than lower doses, and some species more effective than others. As is 
the nature of systematic reviews, we found significant heterogeneity in study designs and 
population, severity of illness of the study group, antibiotics administered, as well as probiotic 
species and strains used, dose, timing and duration of probiotic administration. It may be 
important to note that our sub-group analysis of low baseline risk studies failed to find a 
statistically significant effect of probiotics. Therefore our overall effect estimate may not be 
directly applicable to clinical scenarios with inherent lower baseline risk of AAD. Using the 
GRADE criteria [25], the quality of the evidence included in our meta-analysis was moderate 
and therefore it would be appropriate to base future clinical practice on our results.
Our results show evidence of a placebo effect, with a reduction in risk of AAD of 31% when 
probiotics were compared to placebo, but 65% when probiotics were compared to no 
treatment. Placebo effect is not well understood but this could be attributed to expectations of 
symptom change with neurobiological underpinnings and actual effects on the brain and body 
[69]. This effect could be investigated further in well-designed, three-armed, RCTs.

17
Secondary objectives included sub-group analyses of dose-response and species-specific 
response. In studies where dosages of the same species were compared [38,43,49,66], higher 
doses showed a significantly greater benefit (RR=0.54). It is difficult to interpret the dosage 
effect as the four studies that compared different doses of the same probiotic species made 
comparisons of differing magnitudes. Probiotic course duration was reported in most studies 
(40 out of 42), ranging from five to 56 days. Most commonly, probiotics were administered for 
the duration of antibiotic therapy plus a further seven days, or a total of 14 days. It would be 
biologically plausible to suggest that probiotic use should be continued for some period after 
the cessation of antibiotics. This is another question worth investigating in future trials.
Many studies used blends of probiotic species and strains, which made it problematic to 
establish independent associations. In our sub-group analyses, the individual probiotic 
species that demonstrated the greatest effect sizes were 
B. licheniformis (1 study, RR=0.39), 
B. longum (4 studies, RR=0.46) and B. subtilis (1 study, RR=0.35). Although demonstrating a 
more moderate effect size, L. acidophilus  (18 studies, RR=0.66), L. casei  (11 studies, 
RR=0.59) and S. boulardii (9 studies, RR=0.63) were used in many more studies. Overall, the 
lactobacillus genus showed a good effect with a small confidence interval. The individual 
species L. acidophilus was used in the greatest number of studies, demonstrating a moderate 
effect with a relatively small confidence interval. Moderate effect sizes were noted with other 
species and strains, which may be worth looking into more specifically in future trials. L. 
helveticus, L. plantarum, L. reuteri, B. bifidum, S. thermophilus and C. butyricum did not show 
evidence of effectiveness in reducing incidence of AAD. 
We found only one study [68] comparing two strains of the same probiotic species, L. casei 
DN-114001, (Actimel®) and L. casei Shirota (Yakult). In this study L. casei DN-114001 was 
significantly more effective for preventing AAD than L. casei Shirota . However, we were 
unable to include this data in our review as it was not randomised. Future RCTs should focus 
on direct comparisons of single or combined probiotic species and strains.
The most commonly identified indication for antibiotics was treatment of H. pylori . The 
reduction in diarrhoeal side effects by 45%, through the use of adjunct probiotics, may be a 
significant finding in improving quality of life for these patients.
Limitations
Page 18 of 48

For peer review only
18
A limitation of this study is that the only outcome measured was incidence of diarrhoea. This 
review’s utility in clinical practice may have been improved by also analysing duration of AAD, 
diarrhoea severity, need for hospitalisation due to diarrhoea and quality of life measures. 
Additionally, it may have been informative to correlate outcomes with the duration of probiotic 
course or the date of probiotic initiation in relation to antibiotics.
Sub-group analysis by antibiotic would have been informative but was not possible as many 
of the included studies did not state the antibiotic name, class, route of administration, dose 
or course length that participants were administered. Future studies could focus on this.
This study was somewhat limited in scope as we only included studies published in English. 
Additionally, the initial search was a title search as opposed to keyword search, which may 
explain the lower number of studies initially identified, compared to the recent Cochrane 
review [20].
Agreements and disagreements with other studies
This study is concordant with findings from the aforementioned Cochrane systematic review 
[20]. Goldenberg found that probiotics led to a significant reduction in incidence of AAD from 
18% to 12% of participants (R 0.58, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.70). The present review included 18 
additional studies (4487 additional participants). This increase in total population increases 
the power of our review to detect smaller clinically relevant differences between groups in 
incidence of AAD. 
Our sub-group analyses found similarly to one previous meta-analysis [70] that 
Lactobacillus 
and Saccharomyces genera reduced incidence of AAD. A more recent meta-analysis [71] 
found, also concordantly, that many Lactobacillus and Bifidobacteria species and S. boulardii 
were effective. Previous meta-analyses have not reported on dose-response. 
Our sub-group analyses were also in agreement with The American Gastroenerological 
Association Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Role of Probiotics in the Management of 
Gastrointestinal Disorders [72] which suggest the use of S. boulardii; or the 2-strain 
combination of L. acidophilus CL1285 and L. casei LBC80R among other probiotic species for 
prevention of AAD.
Contrary to the findings of our review, one meta-analysis [73] reported that probiotics may not 
be effective in reducing the incidence of AAD, however, only 13 studies were analysed, 
Page 19 of 48
For peer review only - http://bmjopen.bmj.com/site/about/guidelines.xhtml
BMJ Open

19
including adults over 65 only. This suggests a need for looking separately at the effectiveness 
of probiotics in populations of younger and older adults.
CONCLUSIONS
This review found evidence supporting a moderate protective effect for probiotics in preventing 
AAD. In absolute terms, the NNT, to prevent one case of AAD would be 20 patients. These 
results should be applied with caution in clinical scenarios with inherent lower baseline risk of 
AAD. In studies that compared dosage of the same probiotic higher doses were found to be 
significantly more effective, suggesting a recommended dose of over 10 billion cfu per day. 
Although the probiotic species that demonstrated the greatest effect were B. licheniformis, B. 
longum, and B. subtilis, each was only studied in a handful of trials. The species L. acidophilus, 
L. casei and S. boulardii, still demonstrating moderate effect sizes in preventing AAD, were 
used in many more trials. A good effect size was found supporting the use of probiotics, given 
concurrently with antibiotics for H. pylori eradication therapy. 
This review has demonstrated overall effectiveness of probiotics for the prevention of AAD, 
including a dose-response and some species-specific effectiveness of probiotics. Further 
high-quality trials are needed, focusing on direct comparison of doses, comparison of 
individual species and combinations of species. Future studies should record not only 
incidence of diarrhoea, but also duration, severity, quality of life measures and length of stay 
in hospital so that an assessment of the cost-benefit of probiotic therapy can be made. Future 
trials should ensure there is adequate blinding and reporting of adverse events.

ETHICS APPROVAL 
This systematic review and meta-analysis was based on published data. As researchers did 
not access any information that could lead to the identification of an individual patient, no 
concerning ethical issue was raised in this research. Therefore, obtaining ethical approval and 
consent of participants was waived.

Supplemental Files  
  
Supplemental file 1: Original study protocol  
  
Review title  
Probiotics for the prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea: A systematic review and meta-analysis   
  
Anticipated or actual start date  
08/08/2019  
  
Anticipated completion date  
30/05/2021  
  
Named contact  
Clare Goodman  
  
Named contact email

The University of Notre Dame Australia School of Medicine Sydney Campus, School of

88-90 Water Street  
Auburn, NSW, AUS 2144

The University of Notre Dame Australia School of Medicine Sydney Campus, School of Medicine

NA  
  
Conflicts of interest  
None known  
  
Collaborators  
NA  
  
Review question(s)  
(1) Do probiotics reduce the incidence of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in adults?  
(2) Is there a dose-response?  
(3) Is there a species-specific response?  
  
Searches  
Databases to be searched: CINAHL Plus, EMBASE, MEDLINE (Ovid), Web of Science and Google Scholar from inception to 
May 2021, as well as a manual search of clinical trial registries and the reference lists of relevant systematic reviews.  
Additional details about the search strategy can be found in the attached full search strategy.

For peer review only
  
Condition or domain being studied  
Antibiotics are one of the most commonly prescribed medications. They disturb the normal gastrointestinal microbiota, 
which can lead to diarrhoea. Probiotics are live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a 
health benefit on the host. Our objective was to evaluate existing evidence for the use of probiotics in preventing 
antibioticassociated diarrhoea (AAD) in adults.  
  
Participants/population  
Inclusion: Studies of participants 18 years or older who were receiving any antibiotic therapy for any reason  
Exclusion: Studies with participants younger than 18  
  
Intervention(s), exposure(s)  
Probiotics - any species/strain, dose or formulation   
  
Comparator(s)/control  
Placebo, alternative dose, alternative probiotic strain, or no treatment control  
  
Outcome measure(s)  
Incidence of diarrhoea as defined by authors during the antibiotic treatment or follow-up phases  
Studies were excluded if they examined probiotics only for treatment, rather than prevention, of AAD  
  
Types of study to be included  
Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) only   
Written in English  
  
Context  
Any setting: inpatient or outpatient  
  
Data extraction (selection and coding)  
Data will be extracted from each article by two of three of the authors (CG, GK, KL), using a standardised data extraction 
form following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta -Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. This will be 
housed within Covidence online software (Covidence systematic review software, Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, 
Australia. Available at www.covidence.org). Data items collected to be included:  number of patients allocated to each group, 
probiotic species, formulation, dose and regime, whether a placebo or ‘nothing‘ control was used, and outcome data on 
incidence of AAD.  
  
Risk of bias (quality) assessment  
Risk of bias will assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias [24] tool within the Covidence online software. Assessment will be 
conducted by two of three authors (CG, GK, KL) and discrepancies resolved by consensus.  
  
Strategy for data synthesis  
For data analysis we will use the RevMan 5.4.1 statistical software (Review Manager (RevMan) [Computer program]. 
Version 5.4. The Cochrane Collaboration, 2020.) We will use either a fixed-effects or random-effects model, reported as 
either odds ratios or risk ratios with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). The number needed to treat (NNT) 
will also calculated for the complete case analysis.  
  
Analysis of subgroups or subsets  
Our a priori clinical heterogeneity variables will include probiotic dose and probiotic species.  
  
Type and method of review  
Systematic review and meta-analysis

PRISMA 2009 Checklist 
Section/topic  # Checklist item  Reported 
on page #  
TITLE   
Title  1 Identify the report as a systematic review, meta-analysis, or both.  1 
ABSTRACT   
Structured summary  2 Provide a structured summary including, as applicable: background; objectives; data sources; study eligibility criteria, 
participants, and interventions; study appraisal and synthesis methods; results; limitations; conclusions and 
implications of key findings; systematic review registration number.  
2 
INTRODUCTION   
Rationale  3 Describe the rationale for the review in the context of what is already known.  4 
Objectives  4 Provide an explicit statement of questions being addressed with reference to participants, interventions, comparisons, 
outcomes, and study design (PICOS).  
4 
METHODS   
Protocol and registration  5 Indicate if a review protocol exists, if and where it can be accessed (e.g., Web address), and, if available, provide 
registration information including registration number.  
Appendix 
Eligibility criteria  6 Specify study characteristics (e.g., PICOS, length of follow-up) and report characteristics (e.g., years considered, 
language, publication status) used as criteria for eligibility, giving rationale.  
5 
Information sources  7 Describe all information sources (e.g., databases with dates of coverage, contact with study authors to identify 
additional studies) in the search and date last searched.  
5 
Search  8 Present full electronic search strategy for at least one database, including any limits used, such that it could be 
repeated.  
5 / 
Appendix  
Study selection  9 State the process for selecting studies (i.e., screening, eligibility, included in systematic review, and, if applicable, 
included in the meta-analysis).  
5 
Data collection process  10 Describe method of data extraction from reports (e.g., piloted forms, independently, in duplicate) and any processes 
for obtaining and confirming data from investigators.  
5 
Data items  11 List and define all variables for which data were sought (e.g., PICOS, funding sources) and any assumptions and 
simplifications made.  
5 
Risk of bias in individual 
studies  
12 Describe methods used for assessing risk of bias of individual studies (including specification of whether this was 
done at the study or outcome level), and how this information is to be used in any data synthesis.  
5 
Summary measures  13 State the principal summary measures (e.g., risk ratio, difference in means).  5 
Synthesis of results  14 Describe the methods of handling data and combining results of studies, if done, including measures of consistency 
(e.g., I2) for each meta-analysis.

intervention group (b) effect estimates and confidence intervals, ideally with a forest plot.

key groups (e.g., healthcare providers, users, and policy makers).

identified research, reporting bias).
