1 
 
PEER REVIEW HISTORY 
BMJ Open publishes all reviews undertaken for accepted manuscripts. Reviewers are asked to 
complete a checklist review form (http://bmjopen.bmj.com/site/about/resources/checklist.pdf) and 
are provided with free text boxes to elaborate on their assessment. These free text comments are 
reproduced below.   
 
ARTICLE DETAILS 
 
TITLE (PROVISIONAL) Probiotics for the prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea: A 
systematic review and meta-analysis 
AUTHORS Goodman, Clare; Keating, Georgia; Georgousopoulou, Ekavi; 
Hespe, Charlotte; Levett, Kate 
 
 
VERSION 1 – REVIEW 
 
REVIEWER SZAJEWSKA, Hania 
The Medical University of Warsaw, Dept of Paediatrics 
REVIEW RETURNED 29-Oct-2020 
 
GENERAL COMMENTS The manuscript ‘Probiotics for the prevention of antibiotic-
associated diarrhoea: A systematic review and meta-analysis’ 
aims to update current evidence on this topic. The research 
question is clear and clinically important. The authors analysed a 
substantial amount of evidence and provided clear conclusions. 
There are, however, numerous issues which negatively impact the 
manuscript’s credibility and consistency. 
 
General comments 
1. The authors decided to choose statistical model (i.e. fixed vs. 
random effects) depending on heterogeneity of the results. 
However, Cochrane Handbook clearly states that ‘The choice 
between a fixed-effect and a random-effects meta-analysis should 
never be made on the basis of a statistical test for heterogeneity’ 
(chapter 10.10.4). 
2. The authors state, that their main outcome was “incidence of 
AAD, classified as three or more episodes of loose stools (5-7 
Bristol Stool Scale), in any 24-hour period during the antibiotic 
treatment or follow-up phases.” Please clarify whether all included 
trials reported the outcome as stated above, including the use of 
Bristol Stool Scale. At least one study documented that there is a 
proven, large outcome heterogeneity in studies on AAD [doi: 
10.1371/journal.pone.0228824]. 
3. The authors have chosen odds ratios as a method of presenting 
intervention effects. The Cochrane Handbook states that odds and 
odds ratios are more difficult to interpret for a reader. Please 
consider presenting the results as risk ratios. 
4. Throughout the manuscript, the terms ‘diarrhea’ and ‘AAD’ are 
used interchangeably. Please standardize the terminology in this 
respect. 
5. The term ‘flora’ used throughout the manuscript is historical, and 
should be replaced by ‘microbiota’. Also, C. difficile no longer 
belongs to Clostridium genus, but to Clostridioides, and should be 
renamed in the manuscript accordingly. 
6. Throughout the manuscript, the authors refer to Joshua 
Goldenberg’s 2013 systematic review as the ‘most recent’ 
2 
 
Cochrane review. However, there was an update of this work by 
the same author in 2017. Please revise. 
7. The database search was performed over a year ago. A search 
update is highly recommended. 
Section-specific comments 
Abstract: 
8. “…co-administration of probiotics reduces the risk of antibiotic-
associated diarrhoea in adults by 46% (Odds ratio (OR)=0.54 
[95% CI: 0.44, 0.67], p<0.00001)” – risk and odds are two entirely 
different things. This sentence needs rephrasing. 
9. “Probiotics are non-pathogenic live micro-organisms, thought to 
improve the microbial balance of the host and reduce colonisation 
by pathogenic bacteria.” – the definition presented by the authors 
is different from the widely adopted ISAPP definition 
(https://isappscience.org/for-scientists/resources/probiotics/). 
Please revise in the Abstract and Introduction. 
10. ‘Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis.’ Please revise 
to precisely state ‘systematic review and meta-analysis of 
randomized-controlled trials’. 
Introduction: 
11. “It is estimated that the increase in hospital admission due to 
AAD is 3.6 to 21.3 days” – hospital admissions cannot be 
measured in days, in contrast to hospital stay. Please revise. 
12. “They can be delivered orally, adhere to target gastrointestinal 
epithelium and are stable in acid and bile (Dunne et al. 2001).” – 
this statement seems to be a slight oversimplification of our current 
understanding of probiotics’ mechanism of action. In fact, in many 
cases this mechanism is unknown. According to ISAPP, ‘In some 
cases, probiotic mechanisms of action are known; in other cases, 
they are not even though a health benefit has been demonstrated. 
A common misconception is that probiotics need to alter the gut 
microbiota in order to be effective. In fact, probiotics are not known 
to take up permanent residence in the gut despite documented 
health benefits.’ 
13. ‘One of the most expensive probiotics in Australia costs less 
than four dollars daily (VSL#3 AU$3.96 per day, available from 
NourishMeOrganics.com.au, April 2020).’ – usually, use of 
commercial product names is discouraged in articles. Please refer 
to BMJ Open author guidelines on this subject. 
 
Methods: 
14. The authors state, that “a sensitivity analysis was performed”. 
However, it is not described what kind of a sensitivity analysis it 
precisely was. Please clarify. 
15. “Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing probiotic use 
(any strain, dose or formulation) to placebo, alternative dose, 
alternative probiotic strain, or no treatment, for the prevention of 
diarrhoea in adults receiving antibiotic therapy were eligible for 
inclusion in this review.” There is a discrepancy between this part 
and the abstract, which states that only ‘placebo or no treatment 
control’ will be taken into an account. Please clarify. 
 
Results: 
16. “A total of 346 articles were identified in the initial search, of 
which 53 were eligible for fulltext review, and 37 of those articles 
were eligible for inclusion in the study.” – if so, this search strategy 
has impressive specificity, considering that in recent Cochrane 
review mentioned previously, as much as 1351 studies were 
identified from the primary electronic databases. This surprisingly 
low number should be at least commented on in the discussion 
3 
 
17. There are some missing data in Table 1, e.g. in column 2 of 
references 31-33, in column 5 of reference 32. 
18. “All studies reported the outcome of interest; incidence of AAD 
as measured by three or more occurrences of diarrhoea in a 24-
hour period”. Firstly, I think that this sentence should read 
“occurences of loose stool” rather than “occurences of diarrhoea”. 
Secondly, in reference to my previous comment – did really all 
those authors use Bristol Stool Scale? Haven’t you identified at 
least one trial which used different definition of diarrhoea, or didn’t 
use any definition at all? Or perhaps, did you exclude trials which 
didn’t provide a precise definition of diarrhoea? 
19. “Overall 51% of studies were rated as having a low risk of bias, 
while 49% were at unclear risk of bias.” What were the criteria for a 
study to be ranked as “low” or “high” risk of bias? 
20. “…demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in the 
incidence of AAD by 46% (Odds ratio (OR)=0.54 [95% CI: 0.44, 
0.67], p<0.00001).” – similar comment as before – incidence and 
odds are two different things. Please revise throughout the 
manuscript for consistency. 
21. “This suggests that the number needed to treat (NNT), to 
prevent one case of AAD would be 19 patients.” – how was NNT 
calculated? On the basis of OR? If so, then according to Cochrane 
Handbook, the authors should provide an information and rationale 
on the ‘assumed comparator risk’ (chapter 15.4.4.). 
22. “On inspection, the funnel plot of the complete case analysis 
(Figure 3) shows little evidence of publication bias. This suggests 
that our results are robust to theoretical large future trials with 
results in the opposite direction (i.e. that probiotics increase the 
risk of AAD rather than decreasing it).” – I don’t understand, how 
low risk of publication bias translates to robustness of results to 
future studies with different results. Also, visually, the funnel plot is 
not necessarily symmetric – there are six small studies (SE>1) with 
results more favourable towards probiotics compared to only 2 
small studies on the right side of the plot. Did you consider 
performing tests for asymmetry? 
23. “No serious adverse events were reported in any of the 
included studies” – it would be also useful to include information, 
how many studies reported adverse events at all. 
 
Discussion 
24. The results should be briefly recapped rather than rewritten 
completely with p-values, confidence intervals etc. Please revise. 
25. Some information regarding the results is presented for the first 
time, eg. “we found significant heterogeneity between study 
designs and population, severity of illness of the study group, as 
well as probiotic species used, dose, timing and duration of 
probiotic administration.”, or “In the five RCTs investigating adjunct 
probiotic use with antibiotics for H.pylori treatment we found a 
reduction in diarrhoeal side-effects (OR=0.43, [95% CI: 0.27, 0.69], 
p<0.001).”. Data like this should be introduced in the “results” 
section, and only recapped or commented on in the discussion. 
26. “One study [62] compared two strains of L. casei, Actimel® ( L. 
casei DN-114001 ) and Yakult® ( L. casei Shirota ), for the 
prevention of AAD. In this study L. casei DN-114001 was 
significantly more effective than L. casei Shirota , however, we 
were unable to include this data in our review as it was not 
randomised.” – I don’t understand, why this specific study is 
mentioned? I don’t think that it contributes much to the discussion. 
I guess there were more studies excluded for similar reasons, so 
why mention this one? 
4 
 
27. “A limitation of this study is that the only outcome measured 
was incidence of diarrhoea. This review’s utility in clinical practice 
may have been improved by also analysing duration of AAD.” – 
this is a very important point, however I would also add for 
consideration: diarrhea severity, need for hospitalization due to 
diarrhoea, quality of life and other outcomes of real-life importance. 
Considering the fact, that the definition of diarrhoea in the included 
trials was ‘3 or more loose stools in 24 h’, it might turn out that 
majority of AAD cases were mild, transient and without a real 
impact on patient’s comfort. This needs to be emphasized more. 
28. The authors focused on certain species effectiveness, however 
it is known that probiotic effects are not only species-, but also 
strain-dependent. Please comment on it in the discussion. 
 
REVIEWER Vargas, Ashley 
National Institute of Child Health and Human Development 
REVIEW RETURNED 17-Nov-2020 
 
GENERAL COMMENTS This is a very clear, easy to follow systematic review and meta-
analysis of probiotic use to prevent AAD. I have three 
concerns/requests: 
1) I do not see a strength of evidence analysis. This is a must to 
understand how confidence the scientific community is in the 
results a systematic review, please complete this. 
2) Please explain the scientific rationale for allowing “no treatment” 
as a reasonable control group. Consider excluding these studies 
on the basis of an inappropriate comparison group. 
3) Did response vary by antibiotic name, type, route of 
administration, length or dose? Since probiotics would be 
preventing a side-effect of an antibiotic and since diarrheal 
response varies by antibiotic – I would highly encourage the 
authors complete some subgroup analysis with respect to the 
antibiotic used as they are able given the data available from each 
study. 
 
Minor comments: 
In the abstract please state the strength of evidence found 
(moderate?) 
Pg 4 line 52 – reword for clarity and consider – only certain 
species… were found to be effective 
Pg 12 line 33 – please state the strength of the evidence and 
update your methods regarding how you determined the strength 
of the evidence 
Pg 14 line 14 – did all studies attempt to capture and report on 
adverse events? If so, please state this, if not clarify how many 
studies did not attempt to capture or report on adverse events. 
Please add to the discussion the relevance of these findings to 
major medical association positions on use of probiotics including 
AGA (https://www.gastrojournal.org/article/S0016-5085(20)34729-
6/fulltext) 
 
REVIEWER Goldenberg, Joshua  
National University of Natural Medicine, Helfgott Research 
Institute 
REVIEW RETURNED 20-Nov-2020 
 
GENERAL COMMENTS This is a well written paper overall and the authors are to be 
commended. There are a few issues outstanding that should be 
addressed. 
5 
 
 
Major issues: In applying a published quality 'checklist' to this 
review (AMSTAR2) this review would be rated at "Critically Low 
Quality". This is primarily due to issues in four critical domains: 1. 
Search: a grey literature was not searched, studies were limited to 
English and a justification for this is not given (AMSTAR2 item 4). 
2. I did not see a list of excluded studies nor a justification for 
exclusions (AMSTAR2 item 7). 3. While the authors report on risk 
of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool they do not explore 
how this might impact the overall results of the study (AMSTAR2 
item 13). In other words there is no sensitivity analysis using low 
risk fo bias studies only for example. 4. There does not appear to 
be an a priori protocol (AMSTAR2 item 2). 
Non critical domains: 1. I don't see where the authors reported on 
the sources of funding for the included studies (MSTAR2 item 10). 
 
Other issues: 
Publication bias: while the authors conducted a funnel plot visual 
assessment they did not conduct any formal statistical tests such 
as Eggers regression. This is not essential but could be added if 
the authors wish. 
The search is 'stale' it was conducted >1 year ago and should be 
updated and the overall results updated before publication. 
Heterogeneity is discussed but not explored. 
Subgroups have no statement or evaluation for credibility (e.g. 
ICEMAN) and should not be presented in the abstract unless very 
credible. 
There seems to be some confusion with Risk of Bias. The 
domains of "Selective outcome reporting" and "Missing outcome 
data" seem to be conflated.   
 
REVIEWER Abner, Sophia  
University of Leicester, College of Health Sciences 
REVIEW RETURNED 04-Feb-2021 
 
GENERAL COMMENTS The aims of the systematic review and meta-analysis are clear 
and the statistical methods used for the meta-analysis are in line 
with the study objectives. 
Specifically, the method to use random effects where there is high 
heterogeneity is correct. The authors state they will use fixed 
effects where heterogeneity is low but the use of this has not been 
indicated. The authors have also considered the limitations of their 
study in the review in regards to the different strains of probiotic 
species, varying dosage amounts, and difference in comparison 
groups by performing subgroup analyses. I2 statistics have been 
provided along with odds ratios and their corresponding 95% 
confidence intervals and p-values, and a funnel plot. A sensitivity 
analysis was also performed. 
There are some minor comments the authors may wish to 
address. In two of the sub group analyses the I2 statistic has not 
been reported and the type of model used is not stated (probiotic 
dose and probiotic strain). Additionally it may be beneficial to 
include the results of the sensitivity analysis in the supplementary 
material and report the p-value of the funnel plot. 
Overall, the statistical methodology in this systematic review and 
meta-analysis has been well thought out and the limitations of their 
review have been addressed through using sub group analyses.   
 
 
6 
 
 
VERSION 1 – AUTHOR RESPONSE 
 
Reviewer: 1 
Prof. Hania SZAJEWSKA, The Medical University of Warsaw 
Comments to the Author: 
The manuscript ‘Probiotics for the prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea: A systematic review 
and meta-analysis’ aims to update current evidence on this topic. The research questi on is clear and 
clinically important. The authors analysed a substantial amount of evidence and provided clear 
conclusions. There are, however, numerous issues which negatively impact the manuscript’s 
credibility and consistency. 
 
Reply: We would like to thank the Reviewer for their time and effort to review our work and provide 
feedback that increased the quality of our research output.  
 
General comments 
1.      The authors decided to choose statistical model (i.e. fixed vs. random eff ects) depending on 
heterogeneity of the results. However, Cochrane Handbook clearly states that ‘The choice between a 
fixed-effect and a random-effects meta-analysis should never be made on the basis of a statistical 
test for heterogeneity’ (chapter 10.10.4). 
 
Reply: We would like to thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have updated our statistical analysis 
to use a random effects model due to significant heterogeneity between study participant age groups, 
probiotic species and doses and protocols implemented and difference in outcome measurement. This 
decision was purely based on the studies’ methodological differences and not on statistical tests.  
 
2.      The authors state, that their main outcome was “incidence of AAD, classified as three or more 
episodes of loose stools (5-7 Bristol Stool Scale), in any 24-hour period during the antibiotic treatment 
or follow-up phases.” Please clarify whether all included trials reported the outcome as stated above, 
including the use of Bristol Stool Scale.  At least one study documented that there is a proven, large 
outcome heterogeneity in studies on AAD [doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0228824].  
 
Reply: We have added a sentence describing the heterogeneity of the definition of AAD used. Please 
see page 7 under “Subgroup and heterogeneity analysis”.  
 
3.      The authors have chosen odds ratios as a method of presenting intervention effects. The 
Cochrane Handbook states that odds and odds ratios are more difficult to interpret for a reader. 
Please consider presenting the results as risk ratios. 
 
Reply: We have updated our analysis to use risk ratios as all studies were RCTs and therefore 
prospective 
 
4.      Throughout the manuscript, the terms ‘diarrhea’ and ‘AAD’ are used interchangeably. Please 
standardize the terminology in this respect.  
7 
 
 
Reply: The terminology has now been standardised to the use of term AAD throughout the manuscript.  
 
5.      The term ‘flora’ used throughout the manuscript is historical, and should be replaced by 
‘microbiota’. Also, C. difficile no longer belongs to Clostridium genus, but to Clostridioides, and should 
be renamed in the manuscript accordingly. 
Reply: We have performed these suggested amendments in the revised manusc ript. 
 
6.      Throughout the manuscript, the authors refer to Joshua Goldenberg’s 2013 systematic review 
as the ‘most recent’ Cochrane review. However, there was an update of this work by the same author 
in 2017. Please revise. 
 
Reply: We would like to thank the reviewers for highlighting this issue. We have updated our reference 
to this Cochrane review throughout our review. 
 
7.      The database search was performed over a year ago. A search update is highly recommended.  
 
Reply: We have updated the searc h and added seven studies to the review as requested. Changes 
are made throughout the updated manuscript (methods, results, graphs and tables).  
 
Section-specific comments 
 
Abstract: 
 
8.      “…co-administration of probiotics reduces the risk of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in adults by 
46% (Odds ratio (OR)=0.54 [95% CI: 0.44, 0.67], p<0.00001)” –  risk and odds are two entirely 
different things. This sentence needs rephrasing. 
 
Reply: The manuscript and the abstract have been revised to only use Risk Ratios. Please see updated 
abstract.   
 
9.       “Probiotics are non-pathogenic live micro-organisms, thought to improve the microbial balance 
of the host and reduce colonisation by pathogenic bacteria.” – the definition presented by the authors 
is different from the widely adopted ISAPP definition (https://isappscience.org/for-
scientists/resources/probiotics/). Please revise in the Abstract and Introduction. 
 
Reply: We would like to thank the reviewer for the suggestion. The Abstract and Introduction have been 
revised as per Reviewer’s suggestion. Please see pages 2 and 3. 
8 
 
 
10.     ‘Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis.’ Please revise to precisely state ‘systematic 
review and meta-analysis of randomized-controlled trials’. 
Introduction: 
 
Reply: We have corrected this sentence. 
 
11.     “It is estimated that the increase in hospital admission due to AAD is 3.6 to 21.3 days” – 
hospital admissions cannot be measured in days, in contrast to hospital stay. Please revise. 
 
Reply: We have corrected this sentence. Please see page 3, paragraph 4. 
 
12.     “They can be delivered orally, adhere to target gastrointestinal epithelium and are stable in acid 
and bile (Dunne et al. 2001).” – this statement seems to be a slight oversimplification of our current 
understanding of probiotics’ mechanism of action. In fact, in many cases this mechanism is unknown. 
According to ISAPP, ‘In some cases, probiotic mechanisms of action are known ; in other cases, they 
are not even though a health benefit has been demonstrated. A common misconception is that 
probiotics need to alter the gut microbiota in order to be effective. In fact, probiotics are not known to 
take up permanent residence in the gut despite documented health benefits.’ 
 
Reply: We have revised this section. Please see page 3, paragraph 2. 
 
13.     ‘One of the most expensive probiotics in Australia costs less than four dollars daily (VSL#3 
AU$3.96 per day, available from NourishMeOrganics.com.au, April 2020).’ – usually, use of 
commercial product names is discouraged in articles. Please refer to BMJ Open author guidelines on 
this subject. 
 
Reply: We have updated the cost per day and omitted the commercial product information. Please 
see page 3, paragraph 4.  
 
Methods:  
14.     The authors state, that “a sensitivity analysis was performed”. However, it is not described what 
kind of a sensitivity analysis it precisely was. Please clarify.  
 
Reply: We have now discussed the sensitivity analysis further within the manuscript. Please see page 
5, line 2; page 7, line 8; and page 9, paragraphs 2 and 3. 
 
15.     “Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing probiotic use (an y strain, dose or formulation) 
to placebo, alternative dose, alternative probiotic strain, or no treatment, for the prevention of 
diarrhoea in adults receiving antibiotic therapy were eligible for inclusion in this review.” There is a 
9 
 
discrepancy between this part and the abstract, which states that only ‘placebo or no treatment 
control’ will be taken into an account. Please clarify. 
 
Reply: We have clarified this in the manuscript. Please see abstract and page 4, line 2.  
 
Results: 
16.     “A total of 346 articles were identified in the initial search, of which 53 were eligible for full text 
review, and 37 of those articles were eligible for inclusion in the study.” – if so, this search strategy 
has impressive specificity, considering that in recent Cochrane review mentioned previously, as much 
as 1351 studies were identified from the primary electronic databases. This surprisingly low number 
should be at least commented on in the discussion 
 
Reply: One explanation for this lower number of articles identified in the initial search may be that the 
search was conducted as a title search, as opposed to keyword search. This was indicated in our a 
priori protocol. Please see supplemental file containing our protocol. 
 
17.     There are some missing data in Table 1, e.g. in column 2 of references 31-33, in column 5 of 
reference 32.  
 
Reply: We have filled in missing data for reference 33 column 6, but were unable to find any other 
areas of missing data. This may have been a problem with a version of the manuscript yo u were 
viewing. If this is still the case please let us know. Please see revised table 1.  
 
18.     “All studies reported the outcome of interest; incidence of AAD as measured by three or more 
occurrences of diarrhoea in a 24-hour period”. Firstly, I think that this sentence should read 
“occurences of loose stool” rather than “occurences of diarrhoea”. Secondly, in reference to my 
previous comment – did really all those authors use Bristol Stool Scale? Haven’t you identified at least 
one trial which used different definition of diarrhoea, or didn’t use any definition at all? Or perhaps, did 
you exclude trials which didn’t provide a precise definition of diarrhoea? 
 
Reply: We would like to thank the Reviewer for raising this important point. We have added a co lumn 
to revised Table 1 indicating how each study measured diarrhoea. 
 
19.     “Overall 51% of studies were rated as having a low risk of bias, while 49% were at unclear risk 
of bias.” What were the criteria for a study to be ranked as “low” or “high” risk  of bias? 
 
Reply: We have used the Cochrane risk of bias tool. We have presented the complete risk of bias 
summary for readers to see the review authors’ judgement about each risk of bias item for each 
included study. Please see figure 2. 
 
20.     “…demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in the incidence of AAD by 46% (Odds ratio 
10 
 
(OR)=0.54 [95% CI: 0.44, 0.67], p<0.00001).” – similar comment as before – incidence and odds are 
two different things. Please revise throughout the manuscript for consistency. 
 
Reply: We have only used Risk Ratios in the revised manuscript.  
 
21.     “This suggests that the number needed to treat (NNT), to prevent one case of AAD would be 19 
patients.” – how was NNT calculated? On the basis of OR? If so, then according to Cochrane 
Handbook, the authors should provide an information and rationale on the ‘assumed comparator risk’ 
(chapter 15.4.4.). 
 
Reply: We have revised our calculation of NNT to be based on raw data using the online calculator 
found at https://clincalc.com/Stats/NNT.aspx. 
 
22.     “On inspection, the funnel plot of the complete case analysis (Figure 3) shows little evidence of 
publication bias. This suggests that our results are robust to theoretical large future trials with results 
in the opposite direction (i.e. that probiotics increase the risk of AAD rather than decreasing it).” – I 
don’t understand, how low risk of publication bias translates to robustness of results to future studies 
with different results. Also, visually, the funnel plot is not necessarily symmetric – there are six small 
studies (SE>1) with results more favourable towards probiotics compared to only 2 small studies on 
the right side of the plot. Did you consider performing tests for asymmetry? 
 
Reply: Since updating the search we have added additional studies and updated the funnel plot. On 
consultation with our statistician the symmetry of the funnel plot was found to be acceptable.  
 
23.     “No serious adverse events were reported in any of the included studies” – it would be also 
useful to include information, how many studies reported adverse events at all.  
 
Reply: We have included this information in the results section. Please see page 9, paragraph 4.  
 
Discussion 
24.     The results should be briefly recapped rather than rewritten completely with p -values, 
confidence intervals etc. Please revise. 
 
Reply: We have updated the discussion section to reflect the above advice. Please see page 9 -10. 
 
25.     Some information regarding the results is presented for the first time, eg. “we found significant 
heterogeneity between study designs and population, severity of illness of the study group, as well as 
probiotic species used, dose, timing and duration of probiotic administration.”, or “In the five RCTs 
investigating adjunct probiotic use with antibiotics for H.pylori treatment we found a reduction in 
diarrhoeal side-effects (OR=0.43, [95% CI: 0.27, 0.69], p<0.001).”. Data like this should be introduced 
in the “results” section, and only recapped or commented on in the discussion. 
11 
 
 
Reply: We have now introduced both of the above points in the results section (page 7, paragraph 6 
and page 9, paragraph 1) and only commented on them in the discussion.  
 
26.     “One study [62] compared two strains of L. casei, Actimel® ( L. casei DN-114001 ) and Yakult® 
( L. casei Shirota ), for the prevention of AAD. In this study L. casei DN-114001 was significantly more 
effective than L. casei Shirota , however, we were unable to include this data in our review as it was 
not randomised.” – I don’t understand, why this specific study is mentioned? I don’t think that it 
contributes much to the discussion. I guess there were more studies excluded for similar reasons, so 
why mention this one? 
 
Reply: We mentioned this study because it was the only one we found that made a direct comparison 
of strains. We have revised our discussion of this point. Please see page 10, paragraph 5.  
 
27.     “A limitation of this study is that the only outcome measured was incidence of diarrhoea. This 
review’s utility in clinical practice may have been improved by also analysing duration of AAD.” – this 
is a very important point, however I would also add for consideration: diarrhea severity, need for 
hospitalization due to diarrhoea, quality of life and other outcomes of real-life importance. Considering 
the fact, that the definition of diarrhoea in the included trials was ‘3 or more loose stools in 24 h’, it 
might turn out that majority of AAD cases were mild, transient and without a real impact on patient’s 
comfort. This needs to be emphasized more. 
 
Reply: We agree with the Reviewer and we have updated our limitations paragraph to discuss this 
point. Please see page 10, paragraph 7. 
 
28.     The authors focused on certain species effectiveness, however it is known that probiotic effects 
are not only species-, but also strain-dependent. Please comment on it in the discussion. 
 
Reply: We would like to thank the Reviewer for highlighting this. We have updated the discuss ion 
accordingly. Please see page 10, line 1. 
 
Reviewer: 2 
Dr. Ashley Vargas, National Institute of Child Health and Human Development  
Comments to the Author: 
This is a very clear, easy to follow systematic review and meta-analysis of probiotic use to prevent 
AAD. I have three concerns/requests: 
 
1) I do not see a strength of evidence analysis. This is a must to understand how confidence the 
scientific community is in the results a systematic review, please complete this.  
 
Reply: Thank you for your comment. We have now performed a strength of evidence analysis using 
the GRADE criteria. Please see page 4, paragraph 5 and page 9, paragraph 6.  
12 
 
 
2) Please explain the scientific rationale for allowing “no treatment” as a reasonable control group. 
Consider excluding these studies on the basis of an inappropriate comparison group. 
 
Reply: The authors have discussed this point and feel that no treatment is an appropriate control as 
this would be considered “usual care” in clinical practice. 
 
3) Did response vary by antibiotic name, type, route of administration, length or dose? Since 
probiotics would be preventing a side-effect of an antibiotic and since diarrheal response varies by 
antibiotic – I would highly encourage the authors complete some subgroup analysis with respect to 
the antibiotic used as they are able given the data available from each study.  
 
Reply: More than half of the included studies did not list which antibiotics were administered, so we 
were unable to delineate this. Future studies could focus on treatments of specific antibiotics for this 
purpose. Please see page 11, paragraph 1. 
 
Minor comments: 
In the abstract please state the strength of evidence found (moderate?) 
 
Reply: We added this in the abstract. Please see revised abstract. 
 
Pg 4 line 52 – reword for clarity and consider – only certain species… were found to be effective  
 
Reply: The sentence was reworded.   
 
Pg 12 line 33 – please state the strength of the evidence and update your methods regarding how you 
determined the strength of the evidence 
 
Reply: We have now performed a strength of evidence analysis using the GRADE criteria. Please 
see page 4, paragraph 5 and page 9, paragraph 6. 
 
Pg 14 line 14 – did all studies attempt to capture and report on adverse events? If so, please state 
this, if not clarify how many studies did not attempt to capture or report on adverse events.  
 
Reply: We have included this information in the results section. Please see page 9, paragraph 4. 
 
 
13 
 
Please add to the discussion the relevance of these findings to major medical association positions on 
use of probiotics including AGA (https://www.gastrojournal.org/article/S0016-5085(20)34729-6/fulltext) 
 
Reply: We added this information in the revised discussion. Please see page 11, paragraph 5.  
 
Reviewer: 3 
Dr. Joshua  Goldenberg, National University of Natural Medicine 
Comments to the Author: 
This is a well written paper overall and the authors are to be commended. There are a few issues 
outstanding that should be addressed.  
 
Major issues: In applying a published quality 'checklist' to this review (AMSTAR2) this review would be 
rated at "Critically Low Quality". This is primarily due to issues in four critical domains:  
1. Search: a grey literature was not searched, studies were limited to English and a justification for 
this is not given (AMSTAR2 item 4).  
 
Reply: We have now performed a grey literature search. Studies included were limited to English 
because our group only speaks English. Justification was provided in the revised manuscript. Please 
see page 4, line 3. 
 
2. I did not see a list of excluded studies nor a justification for exclusions (AMSTAR2 item 7).  
 
Reply: As this was not a Cochrane review, we were not required to provide a list of excluded studies, 
with justifications for their exclusions, within the submission to BMJ Open. H owever, this information is 
held within the Covidence online software and summarised in the PRISMA flow chart. Please see Figure 
1. 
 
3. While the authors report on risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, they do not explore 
how this might impact the overall results of the study (AMSTAR2 item 13). In other words there is no 
sensitivity analysis using low risk fo bias studies only for example.  
 
Reply: We would like to thank the Reviewer for highlighting this point. We have now included a 
sensitivity analysis. Please see page 7, paragraph 2 and page 9, paragraphs 2 and 3.  
 
4. There does not appear to be an a priori protocol (AMSTAR2 item 2). 
 
Reply: There was an a priori protocol which was submitted and reviewed within the medical school. 
We will include it as a supplementary file. 
 
14 
 
Non critical domains: 1. I don't see where the authors reported on the sources of funding for the 
included studies (MSTAR2 item 10).  
 
Reply: This was discussed by the authors while making their judgement of “other sources of bias” within 
the risk of bias assessment. 
 
 
Other issues:  
Publication bias: while the authors conducted a funnel plot visual assessment they did not con duct 
any formal statistical tests such as Eggers regression. This is not essential but could be added if the 
authors wish.  
 
Reply: Since updating the search we have added additional studies and updated the funnel plot. On 
consultation with our statistician the symmetry of the funnel plot was found to be acceptable and it 
was not felt that any formal statistical tests would provide any further significant information.  
 
 
The search is 'stale' it was conducted >1 year ago and should be updated and the overall  results 
updated before publication.  
 
Reply: We have updated the search and added seven studies to the review as requested. Changes 
are made throughout the updated manuscript (methods, results, graphs and tables).  
 
Heterogeneity is discussed but not explored.  
 
Reply: We have explored heterogeneity, both statistical and methodological, and discussed their 
effects. On this basis we have now chosen to use a random effects model for all analyses.  
 
Subgroups have no statement or evaluation for credibility (e.g. ICEMAN) and should not be presented 
in the abstract unless very credible.  
 
Reply: As per another reviewer’s comment we have now performed a strength of evidence analysis 
using the GRADE criteria. Please see page 4, paragraph 5 and page 9, paragraph 6.  
 
There seems to be some confusion with Risk of Bias. The domains of "Selective outcome reporting" 
and "Missing outcome data" seem to be conflated.  
 
Reply: Thank you for highlighting this issue. We have reviewed this section and made appropriate 
changes in the manuscript. 
15 
 
Reviewer: 4 
Dr.  Sophia   Abner, University of Leicester 
Comments to the Author: 
The aims of the systematic review and meta-analysis are clear and the statistical methods used for 
the meta-analysis are in line with the study objectives. 
 
Specifically, the method to use random effects where there is high heterogeneity is correct. The 
authors state they will use fixed effects where heterogeneity is low but the use of this has not been 
indicated.  
 
Reply: Following Reviewers’ advice, we have de cided to use a random effects model for all analyses 
as there is significant heterogeneity between study methodologies. Please see changes throughout the 
manuscript.  
 
The authors have also considered the limitations of their study in the review in regards  to the different 
strains of probiotic species, varying dosage amounts, and difference in comparison groups by 
performing subgroup analyses. I2 statistics have been provided along with odds ratios and their 
corresponding 95% confidence intervals and p-values, and a funnel plot. A sensitivity analysis was 
also performed. 
There are some minor comments the authors may wish to address. In two of the sub group analyses 
the I2 statistic has not been reported and the type of model used is not stated (probiotic dos e and 
probiotic strain). 
 
Reply: We would like to thank the reviewer for the time they spent to provide productive feedback. We 
have revised our discussion of the I2 statistic in the manuscript and a random effects model was used 
for all analyses due to th e heterogeneity of study methodology. Please see page 7, paragraphs 4 and 
6.  
 
 Additionally it may be beneficial to include the results of the sensitivity analysis in the supplementary 
material and report the p-value of the funnel plot.  
 
Reply: We have included these results in the revised manuscript’s supplementary material as per the 
Reviewer’s suggestion.  
 
Overall, the statistical methodology in this systematic review and meta-analysis has been well thought 
out and the limitations of their review have been addressed through using sub group analyses. 
 
Reply: We would like to thank the Reviewer for their kind words. 
 
 
16

Supplemental Files  
  
Supplemental file 1: Original study protocol  
  
Review title  
Probiotics for the prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea: A systematic review and meta-analysis   
  
Anticipated or actual start date  
08/08/2019  
  
Anticipated completion date  
30/05/2021  
  
Named contact  
Clare Goodman  
  
Named contact email 
ClareLouisaGoodman@gmail.com  
  
Named contact address  
The University of Notre Dame Australia School of Medicine Sydney Campus, School of 
Medicine c/o Dr Kate Levett Auburn Clinical School  
88-90 Water Street  
Auburn, NSW, AUS 2144  
  
Organisational affiliation of the review  
The University of Notre Dame Australia School of Medicine Sydney Campus, School of Medicine  
  
Review team members and their organisational affiliations  
Dr Clare Goodman, The University of Notre Dame Australia School of Medicine Sydney Campus  
Ms Georgia Keating, Alice Springs Hospital, Department of Pharmacy  
Dr Ekavi Georgousopoulou, The University of Notre Dame Australia School of Medicine Sydney Campus  
Dr Charlotte Hespe, The University of Notre Dame Australia School of Medicine Sydney Campus  
Dr Kate Levett, The University of Notre Dame Australia School of Medicine Sydney Campus  
  
Funding sources/sponsors  
NA  
  
Conflicts of interest  
None known  
  
Collaborators  
NA  
  
Review question(s)  
(1) Do probiotics reduce the incidence of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in adults?  
(2) Is there a dose-response?  
(3) Is there a species-specific response?  
  
Searches  
Databases to be searched: CINAHL Plus, EMBASE, MEDLINE (Ovid), Web of Science and Google Scholar from inception to 
May 2021, as well as a manual search of clinical trial registries and the reference lists of relevant systematic reviews.  
Additional details about the search strategy can be found in the attached full search strategy.  
BMJ Publishing Group Limited (BMJ) disclaims all liability and responsibility arising from any reliance
Supplemental material placed on this supplemental material which has been supplied by the author(s) BMJ Open
 doi: 10.1136/bmjopen-2020-043054:e043054. 11 2021;BMJ Open, et al. Goodman C
  
Condition or domain being studied  
Antibiotics are one of the most commonly prescribed medications. They disturb the normal gastrointestinal microbiota, 
which can lead to diarrhoea. Probiotics are live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a 
health benefit on the host. Our objective was to evaluate existing evidence for the use of probiotics in preventing 
antibioticassociated diarrhoea (AAD) in adults.  
  
Participants/population  
Inclusion: Studies of participants 18 years or older who were receiving any antibiotic therapy for any reason  
Exclusion: Studies with participants younger than 18  
  
Intervention(s), exposure(s)  
Probiotics - any species/strain, dose or formulation   
  
Comparator(s)/control  
Placebo, alternative dose, alternative probiotic strain, or no treatment control  
  
Outcome measure(s)  
Incidence of diarrhoea as defined by authors during the antibiotic treatment or follow-up phases  
Studies were excluded if they examined probiotics only for treatment, rather than prevention, of AAD  
  
Types of study to be included  
Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) only   
Written in English  
  
Context  
Any setting: inpatient or outpatient  
  
Data extraction (selection and coding)  
Data will be extracted from each article by two of three of the authors ( CG, GK, KL), using a standardised data extraction 
form following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. This will be 
housed within Covidence online software (Covidence systematic revi ew software, Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, 
Australia. Available at www.covidence.org). Data items collected to be included:  number of patients allocated to each group, 
probiotic species, formulation, dose and regime, whether a pl acebo or ‘nothing‘ control was used, and outcome data on 
incidence of AAD.  
  
Risk of bias (quality) assessment  
Risk of bias will assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias [24] tool within the Covidence online software. Assessment will be 
conducted by two of three authors (CG, GK, KL) and discrepancies resolved by consensus.  
  
Strategy for data synthesis  
For data analysis we will use the RevMan 5.4.1 statistical software (Review Manager (RevMan) [Computer program]. 
Version 5.4. The Cochrane Collaboration, 2020.) We will use either a fixed-effects or random-effects model, reported as 
either odds ratios or risk ratios with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). The number needed to treat (NNT) 
will also calculated for the complete case analysis.  
  
Analysis of subgroups or subsets  
Our a priori clinical heterogeneity variables will include probiotic dose and probiotic species.  
  
Type and method of review  
Systematic review and meta-analysis  
  
  
    
BMJ Publishing Group Limited (BMJ) disclaims all liability and responsibility arising from any reliance
Supplemental material placed on this supplemental material which has been supplied by the author(s) BMJ Open
 doi: 10.1136/bmjopen-2020-043054:e043054. 11 2021;BMJ Open, et al. Goodman C

coli or rhamnosus or acidophilus or bifidum or lactis or bulgaricus or reuteri or casei or thermophilus or boulardii or
